title: Pandas
description: Check the core analyst skill set — load, filter, group, join, and clean.

lessons.title: The two objects everything else uses
lessons.lead: A Series is one labelled column. A DataFrame is a dict of Series sharing one index.

options: A 1D array of values plus an index that labels them
A table with rows and columns
A Python dictionary with a fixed key order
A NumPy array restricted to numbers
questions.explain: Every column of a DataFrame is a Series, and operations between Series align on the index rather than on position.

questions.prompt: What does `df["score"]` return, and what does `df[["name", "score"]]` return?
questions.explain: One column name gives a Series; a list of column names gives a DataFrame — even a list of one.

questions.prompt: Which method should you run first on a dataset you have never seen?
questions.explain: `.info()` tells you the size, the type of every column, and where the missing values are, in one view. `.describe()` and `.head()` come next.

options: `.value_counts()` counts how often each value occurs
`df.head()` permanently trims the DataFrame to 5 rows
questions.explain: `.head()` only shows the first rows — it returns a view for you to look at and leaves `df` alone.

lessons.title: Loading real files
lessons.lead: Reading the file is one line. Reading it correctly is the arguments you pass.

options: Otherwise the index is written as an extra unnamed column
Otherwise the column headers are dropped
It makes the file smaller by compressing it
It is required whenever the file already exists
questions.explain: Forgetting it is why exported files grow an `Unnamed: 0` column every time they round-trip.

questions.prompt: A European CSV export shows every row crammed into one column. What is the likely fix?
options: Convert the file to Excel first
questions.explain: The separator is not always a comma. `sep=";"` handles the common European export.

questions.prompt: Which `read_csv` arguments do what they say?
options: `sheet_name="Term1"` — pick a worksheet from a CSV
questions.explain: `sheet_name` belongs to `read_excel` — a CSV is a single flat file with no sheets.

questions.prompt: What does `pd.read_excel` need that `read_csv` does not?
options: An extra engine package such as openpyxl
The file to be under 10 MB
The columns to be typed in advance
questions.explain: Excel formats need a reader library. `pip install openpyxl` covers .xlsx.

lessons.title: Asking questions of a table
lessons.lead: Select the rows you want, order them, then summarise them per category.

questions.prompt: How do you keep rows where score is at least 50 **and** class is "A"?
questions.explain: Same rule as NumPy: `&` and `|`, with each condition in its own parentheses.

questions.prompt: Why does `df[df.score < 50]["status"] = "retake"` fail to change anything?
options: It assigns into a temporary copy — use a single `.loc` instead
`status` must exist before you can assign to it
String values cannot be assigned this way
questions.explain: That is the SettingWithCopyWarning. Write `df.loc[df["score"] < 50, "status"] = "retake"` — one indexer, one operation.

options: Splits rows by class, then returns the average score for each class
Sorts the table by class and then by score
questions.explain: Split, apply, combine. `.reset_index()` afterwards turns the group labels back into a normal column.

options: `sort_values("score", ascending=False)` puts the highest score first
The original index travels with the rows unless you reset it
`df.nlargest(3, "score")` is a shortcut for the top three
questions.explain: Add `.reset_index(drop=True)` when you want a clean 0..n index after sorting.

lessons.title: Joining tables and handling gaps
lessons.lead: Two operations where a silent mistake changes your numbers without any error message.

questions.prompt: `students` has ids 1, 2, 3 and `scores` has ids 1, 2, 4. How many rows does an inner merge on `id` return?
questions.explain: An inner join keeps only keys present on both sides — ids 1 and 2. `how="left"` would keep all three students, with NaN for Mony.

questions.prompt: A merge returned more rows than you started with. What does that usually mean?
options: The key is not unique on one side
The two tables have different column names
Pandas added the missing rows as NaN
questions.explain: Duplicate keys multiply rows. Check with `df["id"].duplicated().any()` before merging, and always compare the row count afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which command counts missing values per column?
questions.explain: `isna()` gives a boolean table; summing it counts the Trues in each column. Run it before deciding anything.

questions.prompt: Which statements about missing values are true?
options: `dropna(subset=["score"])` drops rows only where score is missing
Filling with the median is safer than the mean when the data is skewed
A column containing NaN becomes a float column
Pandas fills missing numbers with 0 automatically
questions.explain: Nothing is filled automatically — that is the point. Decide deliberately whether to drop or fill, and record the decision.

lessons.title: Working with dates
lessons.lead: Once a column is a real datetime, everything about it becomes available.

options: Turns unparseable values into NaT instead of raising
Guesses the most likely date format
Drops the rows that cannot be parsed
questions.explain: Then `col.isna().sum()` tells you exactly how many values were bad, instead of the load crashing on the first one.

questions.prompt: How do you extract the year from a datetime column?
questions.explain: The `.dt` accessor is the gateway to every date part — `.dt.month`, `.dt.day_name()`, and the rest.

options: The average score for each month
One average for the whole table
questions.explain: resample buckets a datetime index by a frequency. `"ME"` is month-end; the aggregation you chain decides what each bucket becomes.
